title: Chapter 10 Drill: Cognition, Behavior, and Psychiatric Disorders

items.stem: At autopsy of a patient who died with early Alzheimer disease, which brain region is expected to show the earliest neurofibrillary tangle pathology?
options: Primary motor cortex along the precentral gyrus
items.explanation: Neurofibrillary tangle spread in Alzheimer disease follows the Braak stages, beginning in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, then involving the hippocampus and limbic structures, and finally the neocortex. This explains early episodic memory loss. Primary motor, primary visual, and cerebellar cortices are spared until very late, which explains why strength, vision, and coordination remain preserved early in the illness.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar disorder plans pregnancy and asks which of her treatment options carries the greatest risk of neural tube defects and lower child IQ. Which drug is responsible?
items.explanation: Valproate is the most teratogenic common psychotropic and antiseizure drug, causing neural tube defects, craniofacial anomalies, and lower cognitive scores in exposed children, with risk rising with dose. It should be avoided in people who can become pregnant when alternatives exist. Lamotrigine has the lowest malformation rate among mood stabilizers. Lithium is linked to a small increase in cardiac malformations, and quetiapine is not associated with this pattern.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia gains 18 kg in four months after starting a new antipsychotic, and his fasting glucose and triglycerides rise. Which drug is most likely responsible?
items.explanation: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest risk of weight gain, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia among second-generation antipsychotics, through antagonism of histamine H1 and serotonin 5-HT2C receptors. Aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone are considered metabolically neutral or low risk. Baseline and periodic weight, glucose, and lipid monitoring is recommended for all patients, and switching to a lower-risk agent is often the best response.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has an anterior cerebral artery infarct after clipping of an anterior communicating aneurysm. He lies still, speaks only in response to questions, and shows no initiative, although comprehension and strength are preserved. Which region is injured?
options: Left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and frontal pole
Medial frontal and anterior cingulate cortex
items.explanation: Abulia with minimal spontaneous speech or movement and intact comprehension reflects medial frontal and anterior cingulate injury in the anterior cerebral artery territory, which drives motivation. Orbitofrontal damage causes disinhibition and socially inappropriate behavior. Dorsolateral injury impairs planning and working memory. Hippocampal injury produces amnesia but not loss of drive. Dopamine agonists can sometimes improve abulia.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman on lecanemab has new headache and confusion after her third infusion. MRI shows sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity with edema. What is the best next step?
options: Hold further doses and obtain follow-up MRI
Continue the schedule and give acetaminophen
Give alteplase for a presumed stroke
items.explanation: Symptomatic amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema require suspending treatment and repeating MRI until resolution, with clinical monitoring for seizures or focal deficits. Continuing dosing risks progression. Increasing the dose would worsen vascular injury. Thrombolysis is dangerous because the abnormalities reflect vasogenic edema and possible microhemorrhage rather than ischemic stroke, and it can cause fatal bleeding.

items.stem: A 58-year-old accountant has two years of disinhibition, overeating of sweets, loss of empathy, and apathy. Neuropsychological testing shows poor planning and word generation but relatively preserved episodic recall. MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which pattern is characteristic of this disorder?
options: Severe early amnesia with preserved judgment
Prominent visual hallucinations with daily fluctuation of alertness
Executive dysfunction with spared episodic memory
items.explanation: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia presents with personality change, disinhibition, hyperorality, apathy, and executive failure while memory and visuospatial skills stay relatively intact early on. Early prominent amnesia suggests Alzheimer disease. Well-formed hallucinations with fluctuation suggest Lewy body disease. Myoclonus with ataxia in a rapidly progressive illness suggests a prion disorder. Early recognition guides counseling and safety planning for the family.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 120 has a year of slowed thinking, poor concentration, and motor slowing. MRI shows diffuse atrophy with symmetric white matter changes and no mass lesions. What is the best management?
options: Add memantine as primary therapy for cognitive slowing
Start or optimize combination antiretroviral therapy
items.explanation: This picture fits HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, a subcortical syndrome of psychomotor slowing and executive dysfunction. The basis of treatment is effective antiretroviral therapy, with attention to drugs that penetrate the CNS, and symptoms often improve. Memantine has no proven role. Fluconazole would apply only to cryptococcal infection, and radiation would apply to lymphoma, which imaging does not suggest.

items.stem: A 82-year-old man with moderate to severe Alzheimer disease already takes donepezil. His physician adds memantine. What is the mechanism of memantine?
options: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the synapse
items.explanation: Memantine is an uncompetitive, low-affinity NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces excitotoxic glutamate signaling while permitting normal synaptic transmission. It is approved for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease and may be combined with a cholinesterase inhibitor, which works through a different mechanism. Memantine neither inhibits acetylcholinesterase nor acts at nicotinic receptors, and it does not inhibit monoamine oxidase B, the target of selegiline.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has stepwise cognitive decline over three years with slowed processing and gait slowing. MRI shows extensive periventricular white matter hyperintensities and several lacunes. Which measure best slows progression?
options: Daily high-dose vitamin E supplementation for years
Treating blood pressure and vascular risk factors
Long-term estrogen replacement started at age seventy
items.explanation: Subcortical small vessel disease drives vascular cognitive impairment, and the most effective strategy is treating blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, and smoking, with antiplatelet therapy when a stroke has occurred. Vitamin E has no proven benefit in vascular or Alzheimer dementia. Estrogen replacement in older women did not protect cognition and raised dementia risk. Ginkgo biloba failed to prevent decline in large trials.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has a two-week illness with agitation, paranoia, insomnia, then orofacial dyskinesias, seizures, and autonomic instability. Which evaluation is most important?
options: Escalating antipsychotic doses without further testing
CSF NMDA receptor antibodies and a search for teratoma
items.explanation: Psychiatric onset followed by dyskinesias, seizures, decreased consciousness, and dysautonomia in a young woman is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis until proven otherwise. CSF antibody testing is more sensitive than serum, and pelvic imaging seeks an ovarian teratoma, which should be removed. Antipsychotic escalation risks neuroleptic intolerance. Skull films add nothing, and ceruloplasmin alone addresses Wilson disease only.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a six-week history of poor concentration and low mood. She answers many cognitive questions with "I don't know," wakes at 4 AM, and has lost weight. Her MRI is unremarkable for age. What is the best next step?
options: Start donepezil 5 mg nightly for presumed Alzheimer disease
Order amyloid PET immediately before any treatment
Start sertraline, then retest cognition after remission
Begin memantine titration as for moderate dementia
items.explanation: Abrupt onset, effortful but unsuccessful responses, early waking, and weight loss suggest depression with secondary cognitive impairment. Treating the mood disorder and retesting is appropriate because depression can mimic dementia and may also precede it. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine address established dementia, not depression. Amyloid PET is not indicated before the mood disorder is treated.

items.stem: A geriatrics team designs a program to reduce delirium in hospitalized older adults. Which intervention has the best evidence?
options: Routine prophylactic haloperidol for all patients over 75
Reorientation, sleep protection, and early mobilization
Scheduled diphenhydramine every night for sleep
A nightly benzodiazepine for all patients on the ward
items.explanation: Multicomponent nonpharmacologic programs that address orientation, sleep, mobility, hydration, hearing, and vision reduce delirium incidence by roughly a third. Prophylactic antipsychotics have not shown consistent benefit. Diphenhydramine and benzodiazepines are deliriogenic in older adults and should be avoided. Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation that threatens safety. Reviewing medications for deliriogenic drugs is also a standard part of prevention, and treating pain adequately lowers risk.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man has lifelong difficulty with reciprocal conversation, rigid routines, intense narrow interests, and sensory sensitivity. Which statement about diagnosing his condition is correct?
options: Symptoms must begin in early development
Intellectual disability must be present for the diagnosis
The condition resolves completely with maturity into adulthood
items.explanation: Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition requiring persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors, with symptoms beginning in the early developmental period, even if demands exceed capacity only later. Many autistic adults have average or high intelligence, so intellectual disability is not required. It does not resolve with maturity. A detailed developmental history from a family member helps confirm it.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with Down syndrome has a year of declining daily skills, new seizures, and personality change. Which mechanism explains his high risk of this illness?
options: An extra copy of the tau gene on chromosome 17
Duplication of the presenilin 1 gene on chromosome 14
An extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21
Universal carriage of the apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 allele
items.explanation: People with trisomy 21 carry three copies of the APP gene, which leads to amyloid overproduction and Alzheimer pathology in nearly all by age 40, with dementia commonly emerging in the fifties along with late-onset seizures. The tau gene lies on chromosome 17 and is not triplicated. Presenilin 1 lies on chromosome 14 but is not duplicated in Down syndrome. Epsilon 4 carriage is not universal.

items.stem: A 79-year-old retired engineer says he sometimes needs longer to recall names and takes longer to learn new software, but he manages all of his affairs. Which finding is consistent with normal aging?
options: Progressive loss of the ability to manage medications and household bills
Getting lost in a familiar neighborhood
Repeating the same questions within minutes
Slower processing speed with occasional delays in word retrieval
items.explanation: Normal aging brings slower processing speed, reduced multitasking efficiency, and occasional word retrieval delays, while accumulated knowledge and daily function are preserved. Inability to manage medications, disorientation in familiar places, and repetition of questions within minutes reflect functional loss and episodic memory failure, signaling neurocognitive disorder that warrants evaluation. Knowing this boundary prevents both false alarm and missed disease.

items.stem: A hospitalist wants a brief validated bedside tool to identify delirium in a 76-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia who has become inattentive and sleepy. Which instrument is most appropriate?
items.explanation: The Confusion Assessment Method detects delirium by assessing acute onset with fluctuation, inattention, disorganized thinking, and altered level of consciousness, and it has high sensitivity and specificity. The Mini-Cog screens for dementia, the Geriatric Depression Scale for depressive symptoms, and the Clinical Dementia Rating stages known dementia severity. None of these detects fluctuating inattention, the core feature of delirium.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry with bipolar disorder is about to start carbamazepine. Which test should be done first to reduce the risk of severe skin reactions?
items.explanation: HLA-B*1502 is strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in people of Southeast and East Asian ancestry, and testing is advised before starting. HLA-B*5701 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity. Thiopurine methyltransferase activity guides azathioprine dosing, and CYP2D6 phenotype affects drugs such as codeine and some antidepressants. It does not predict this carbamazepine reaction. Testing is not needed for most other ancestries.

items.stem: A family asks whether their father with moderate dementia now needs a guardian. Which statement is correct?
options: The treating neurologist may appoint a guardian by signing a form
Capacity is a single global status covering every decision
A court decides, informed by a capacity assessment
A low MMSE score automatically establishes incompetence
items.explanation: Capacity is a clinical judgment about a specific decision, while competence and guardianship are legal determinations made by a court, usually relying on clinical evidence. Clinicians cannot appoint guardians. Capacity is not global, because a person may manage daily choices yet be unable to consent to complex treatment. No cognitive screening score alone establishes incompetence, and less restrictive options such as powers of attorney are preferred.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable on lithium, develops coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting, and diarrhea after starting ibuprofen for back pain. The lithium level is 2.4 mEq/L. What explains the rise?
items.explanation: Lithium is eliminated almost entirely by the kidney, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazides, and ACE inhibitors reduce its clearance, so levels climb into the toxic range. Lithium is not protein bound and undergoes no hepatic metabolism, so displacement or enzyme inhibition does not apply. Gut absorption is not altered by these drugs. Severe toxicity may require hemodialysis.

items.stem: A 48-year-old former professional football player has impulsivity, mood swings, and worsening memory over several years. He has never had a seizure or stroke. Which neuropathologic finding defines the suspected disease?
options: Perivascular tau deposits at the depths of cortical sulci
Diffuse extracellular amyloid plaques throughout the cortex
Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in the brainstem
Isolated TDP-43 inclusions in the hippocampus
items.explanation: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy follows repetitive head impacts and is defined by patchy, perivascular accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons and astrocytes at the depths of sulci, distinct from the pattern of Alzheimer disease. Diffuse amyloid plaques mark Alzheimer disease. Lewy bodies mark Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia. Isolated hippocampal TDP-43 is seen in limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy. Diagnosis is currently made only at autopsy.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetes has painful peripheral neuropathy and a major depressive episode. Which antidepressant is best for both problems?
options: Bupropion, a norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor
Citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at maximum dose
Duloxetine, a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor
items.explanation: Duloxetine treats depression and is first line for painful diabetic neuropathy, through combined serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition in descending pain pathways. Bupropion and citalopram lack reliable analgesic effects in neuropathy. Mirtazapine improves sleep and appetite but has little proven benefit for neuropathic pain and may cause weight gain, which is unhelpful in diabetes. Liver function and blood pressure should be monitored.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has slowed thinking, distal paresthesias, and macrocytosis. Her serum B12 is borderline at 250 pg/mL. Which test best confirms functional deficiency?
items.explanation: When B12 is borderline, elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirm tissue deficiency, because B12 is a cofactor for conversion of methylmalonyl CoA and for homocysteine remethylation. Folate alone cannot explain the neurologic findings, and folate treatment may mask anemia while neurologic damage progresses. Bone marrow biopsy is unnecessary. The sedimentation rate is nonspecific. Intrinsic factor antibodies can then assess pernicious anemia.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has severe depression with delusions of guilt, refuses food and fluids, and is actively suicidal. She has failed two antidepressants. Which treatment offers the most rapid and reliable response?
items.explanation: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective treatment for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression, especially with suicidality or refusal of food, and response rates exceed 70 percent. Transcranial magnetic stimulation is useful in less severe, nonpsychotic cases. Vagus nerve stimulation acts slowly over months. A third serotonin reuptake inhibitor would delay needed treatment. Memory impairment is the main adverse effect and is usually transient.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease faints twice after donepezil is increased to 10 mg. Her pulse is 44 per minute and the ECG shows sinus bradycardia. Which mechanism best explains the syncope?
options: Enhanced vagal tone from increased synaptic acetylcholine
Blockade of cardiac beta adrenergic receptors
Inhibition of calcium channels in the sinus node
Depletion of norepinephrine stores in cardiac sympathetic nerves
items.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors raise acetylcholine at muscarinic synapses, including the heart, where increased vagal tone slows the sinus node and AV conduction and may cause syncope or heart block. Donepezil does not block beta receptors or calcium channels, and it does not deplete norepinephrine. An ECG is advisable before starting therapy in people with conduction disease, and dose reduction or discontinuation resolves the problem.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has eight months of gradually worsening memory and slowed thinking. She has constipation and fatigue, and her examination is otherwise normal. Which initial laboratory evaluation is most appropriate?
options: CSF 14-3-3 protein and real-time quaking-induced conversion
Brain biopsy of the nondominant frontal lobe
Serum B12, TSH, and basic metabolic panel
Apolipoprotein E genotyping for all patients
items.explanation: The first step in cognitive decline is to exclude common reversible contributors: B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, and metabolic derangements such as hypercalcemia, uremia, and hyponatremia. Prion testing is reserved for rapidly progressive courses. Biopsy is almost never needed. Apolipoprotein E genotyping does not diagnose Alzheimer disease and is not recommended for routine clinical evaluation because the result changes risk, not management.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman recovering from a psychotic episode becomes mute and motionless. She holds her arm in an awkward posture for minutes and resists passive movement with waxy flexibility. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Oral olanzapine with rapid escalation over several days
items.explanation: Mutism, posturing, and waxy flexibility define catatonia, and benzodiazepines are first line, with lorazepam improving symptoms within hours in many patients. Dopamine blockers such as haloperidol and olanzapine can worsen catatonia and raise the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Phenytoin has no role. Electroconvulsive therapy is the next step if benzodiazepines fail. Response is often dramatic, so early recognition matters.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has a gastrointestinal bleed and becomes confused and sleepy. He has asterixis and a normal head CT. Which treatment is first line for his neurologic syndrome?
options: Strict protein restriction for several weeks
Lactulose titrated to two to three soft stools daily
Sedation with lorazepam to control his agitation overnight
items.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy results from ammonia and other gut-derived toxins bypassing a failing liver, and lactulose, with rifaximin added for recurrence, lowers colonic ammonia production. Prolonged protein restriction worsens malnutrition and is no longer advised. Benzodiazepines can precipitate or deepen encephalopathy. Mannitol treats cerebral edema from raised pressure and is not standard here. Bleeding and infection should be treated as precipitants.

items.stem: A 58-year-old attorney with very high premorbid intelligence reports that his memory and multitasking have declined over a year. His MMSE is 29 of 30. What is the best next step?
options: Reassure him and discharge without follow-up
Repeat the MMSE in five years
items.explanation: Brief screens have ceiling effects in educated people, so a near-perfect score cannot exclude early decline. Detailed neuropsychological testing compares performance against estimates of premorbid ability and can detect subtle deficits in memory and executive function. Reassurance ignores a credible complaint. Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated without a diagnosis, and waiting years delays identification of treatable causes.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman on sertraline is given linezolid. Within hours she has agitation, diaphoresis, diarrhea, tremor, hyperreflexia, and inducible clonus. Which agent is the most appropriate adjunct after stopping the offending drugs?
items.explanation: Rapid onset with clonus and hyperreflexia indicates serotonin syndrome, from linezolid, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, combined with an SSRI. After stopping both drugs and giving benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine blocks 5-HT2A receptors. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome and are not effective here, and bromocriptine may worsen serotonin toxicity. Haloperidol could aggravate hyperthermia and rigidity.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman started citalopram three weeks ago. She now has confusion and unsteady gait. Sodium is 121 mmol/L, she is euvolemic, and urine osmolality is high. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Cerebral salt wasting from an intracranial lesion
Adrenal insufficiency from chronic steroid use
items.explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors cause SIADH, especially in older women in the first weeks, producing euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine. Cerebral salt wasting causes volume depletion. Adrenal insufficiency does not fit without a steroid history or hypotension. Primary polydipsia gives dilute urine because antidiuretic hormone is appropriately suppressed. Management is stopping the drug and restricting fluid.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with schizophrenia believes that the doctors, nurses, and a neighbor are all the same persecutor wearing different disguises. Which syndrome describes this belief?
items.explanation: Fregoli syndrome is the delusion that different people are actually a single person, often a persecutor, who changes appearance. Capgras syndrome is the belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor. Cotard syndrome is the delusion that one is dead or lacks organs. Anton syndrome is denial of cortical blindness. Misidentification syndromes occur in psychosis, Lewy body disease, and right hemisphere lesions.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man develops dementia over ten weeks, with startle myoclonus and gait ataxia. MRI diffusion sequences show cortical ribbon restriction. Which CSF test has the highest specificity for the suspected diagnosis?
items.explanation: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, ataxia, and cortical diffusion restriction suggests sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The real-time quaking-induced conversion assay detects misfolded prion seeds with about 90 percent sensitivity and near-complete specificity. The 14-3-3 protein is released with any rapid neuronal injury and gives false positives. Patients do not produce measurable antibodies to prion protein, and diffuse slowing on EEG is nonspecific.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of children in the house, REM sleep behavior disorder, and mild parkinsonism. Which treatment is the best initial option for his hallucinations and cognition?
items.explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies features a marked cholinergic deficit, so cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine often improve hallucinations, attention, and cognition. Haloperidol and risperidone carry a risk of severe neuroleptic sensitivity, with worsened parkinsonism, sedation, and rarely fatal reactions. Benztropine worsens cognition and hallucinations. If an antipsychotic is unavoidable, low-dose quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin are used.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has brief, frequent arm and face jerks lasting seconds, then subacute memory loss and confusion. Serum sodium is 124 mmol/L, and MRI shows medial temporal hyperintensity. Which condition is most likely?
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatremia, and amnesia with medial temporal MRI changes are classic for anti-LGI1 encephalitis, which usually affects older men and responds to immunotherapy. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis begins with psychiatric symptoms in young women. Anti-Hu syndromes are linked to small cell lung cancer, and anti-GAD65 disease is associated with stiff person syndrome and cerebellar ataxia.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man receives intramuscular haloperidol in the emergency department. Within hours he has sustained upward gaze deviation, neck twisting, and jaw tightness. What is the best immediate treatment?
options: Oral baclofen titrated gradually over several days
items.explanation: Acute dystonia occurs within hours to days of dopamine blockade, especially in young men given high-potency antipsychotics, and anticholinergic agents rapidly reverse it. Baclofen is too slow and unproven. Phenytoin treats seizures, which this is not. Dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Airway involvement is rare but laryngeal dystonia needs urgent attention.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man given haloperidol for agitation develops temperature of 40 degrees Celsius, confusion, tachycardia, and a creatine kinase of 9,000 U/L over three days. Which examination finding supports neuroleptic malignant syndrome over serotonin syndrome?
options: Symptom onset within hours of the new drug
items.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days after dopamine blockade, with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and raised creatine kinase. Serotonin syndrome begins within hours, with clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, diarrhea, and hyperactive bowel sounds. Treatment of the first includes stopping the antipsychotic, supportive cooling, and dantrolene or bromocriptine when severe. Creatine kinase and renal function should be followed closely.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman with depression has failed two antidepressant trials. She has no psychosis, no metal in her head, and prefers to avoid anesthesia. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation would target which region?
items.explanation: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for treatment-resistant depression is delivered over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a node in mood-regulating circuits that is underactive in depression. It needs no anesthesia and carries a small seizure risk. The occipital cortex and vermis are not mood targets. Motor cortex stimulation is used for pain or mapping, not major depression.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man after a left parietal stroke speaks fluently with frequent sound substitutions. He understands commands well but cannot repeat "no ifs, ands, or buts." Which lesion best explains this aphasia?
options: Left arcuate fasciculus or supramarginal gyrus
Watershed zone between the left middle and anterior cerebral arteries
items.explanation: Fluent speech with phonemic paraphasias, good comprehension, and disproportionately impaired repetition define conduction aphasia, from injury to the arcuate fasciculus or the supramarginal gyrus that disconnects receptive from expressive language areas. Inferior frontal injury causes nonfluent Broca aphasia. Posterior superior temporal injury causes poor comprehension. Watershed lesions spare repetition in transcortical aphasias. Therapy focuses on repetition and phonemic strategies.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man taking clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia develops fever and a sore throat. His absolute neutrophil count is 400 per microliter. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Hold clozapine and manage severe neutropenia urgently
Continue clozapine and add an oral antibiotic for the throat infection
Halve the clozapine dose and recheck in a month
items.explanation: Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia and agranulocytosis, usually in the first months, so regular absolute neutrophil counts are mandatory. A count below 500 with fever is an emergency requiring drug discontinuation and hematologic care. Continuing the drug or merely lowering the dose allows further marrow suppression. A throat swab alone ignores the life-threatening hematologic risk.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar depression takes valproate and is to begin lamotrigine. Why must lamotrigine be started at a lower dose and titrated more slowly?
options: Valproate induces lamotrigine metabolism and lowers levels
Lamotrigine displaces valproate from albumin and raises its level
Valproate inhibits glucuronidation and raises lamotrigine levels
items.explanation: Valproate inhibits glucuronidation, roughly doubling lamotrigine half-life and exposure, which raises the risk of serious rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Slow titration and a halved starting dose reduce this risk. Induction would lower levels, the opposite of this interaction. Displacement from albumin and impaired absorption are not the mechanism. Enzyme inducers such as carbamazepine lower lamotrigine levels instead.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman with moderate dementia becomes agitated and tries to leave the facility each evening. What is the best first step?
options: Look for pain, infection, and triggers first
Start haloperidol immediately to calm her at night
Schedule lorazepam every evening to promote sleep
Use physical restraints at night for her safety
items.explanation: Behavioral symptoms of dementia usually have a trigger, such as unrecognized pain, urinary infection, constipation, sensory deprivation, or an overstimulating setting, so the first step is evaluating these and applying nonpharmacologic strategies. Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly dementia patients and are reserved for severe distress. Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls, and restraints increase agitation and injury.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with epilepsy and bulimia nervosa has a major depressive episode. Which antidepressant should be avoided because it lowers the seizure threshold?
options: Sertraline, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Mirtazapine, an alpha 2 adrenergic receptor antagonist
Escitalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
items.explanation: Bupropion produces dose-related seizures and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in bulimia or anorexia, where electrolyte disturbance adds risk. Sertraline, escitalopram, and mirtazapine carry little seizure liability at therapeutic doses, and SSRIs are generally preferred in epilepsy. The interaction with enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs should also be checked when selecting an antidepressant. Sertraline is usually a safe first choice in epilepsy.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman taking phenelzine develops a severe throbbing headache, blood pressure of 230/130 mm Hg, and palpitations after a meal of aged cheese and cured meats. What is the mechanism?
options: Excess serotonin from reuptake blockade in the synapse
items.explanation: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors block breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut and liver, so tyramine from aged cheese and cured meats displaces norepinephrine from nerve terminals and precipitates hypertensive crisis. Serotonin syndrome is a different interaction and does not explain the pressor response. Histamine reactions cause flushing, and D2 blockade causes parkinsonism. Phentolamine or similar antihypertensives treat the crisis.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken haloperidol for ten years. He now has repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and chewing movements that distress him. What is the best treatment to add?
items.explanation: These orofacial movements represent tardive dyskinesia from long-term dopamine blockade. VMAT2 inhibitors, valbenazine and deutetrabenazine, reduce the movements by limiting presynaptic dopamine packaging. Anticholinergics such as benztropine can worsen tardive dyskinesia. Raising the haloperidol dose may suppress movements briefly but perpetuates the problem. Propranolol helps akathisia and tremor, not this syndrome. Switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic is also reasonable when feasible.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease refuses a recommended cataract surgery. She accurately repeats the risks and benefits, states a firm choice, and reasons about alternatives, but insists, "My eyes are perfectly fine." Which element of decision-making capacity is impaired?
options: Ability to express a consistent and stable choice
Appreciation of how the facts apply to her
Understanding of the facts that were disclosed to her
items.explanation: Capacity rests on four abilities: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a choice. This patient repeats the facts, so understanding is intact, and she states a stable choice. Her reasoning about alternatives is also preserved. What fails is appreciation, meaning recognition that the information applies to her, which often reflects anosognosia in dementia. Capacity is decision specific and should be assessed for the particular choice.

items.stem: An 81-year-old man becomes confused on the second day after hip surgery. He cannot recite the months backward, drifts between drowsiness and agitation, and sees insects on the wall. Which feature best separates this condition from dementia?
options: Impaired delayed recall of new information
Acute onset with a fluctuating level of attention
items.explanation: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates over hours to days, usually from a medical trigger such as surgery, infection, or medication. Memory loss, naming difficulty, and visuospatial errors occur in both delirium and dementia, so they do not discriminate. Inattention, tested by months backward or digit span, is the core bedside marker and should prompt a search for the precipitant.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has progressive behavioral change, then limb weakness with fasciculations over two years. His father and a sister had frontotemporal dementia with motor neuron disease. Which genetic abnormality is the most likely cause?
options: Hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the C9orf72 gene
CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene
Mutation in the presenilin 2 gene causing early-onset Alzheimer disease
Mutation in the superoxide dismutase 1 gene alone
items.explanation: The C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion is the most common genetic cause of both familial frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and it explains pedigrees with either or both. Huntingtin CAG expansion causes Huntington disease with chorea. Presenilin 2 mutations cause rare early-onset Alzheimer disease. SOD1 mutations cause motor neuron disease without typical frontotemporal dementia. Genetic counseling should be offered to relatives before any testing.

items.stem: A neurologist reviews candidates for an anti-amyloid antibody. Which genotype carries the highest risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities?
items.explanation: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, which include edema and microhemorrhage, occur most often in people who carry the epsilon 4 allele, with the greatest risk in homozygotes, probably because of heavier vascular amyloid deposition. Epsilon 2 is protective against Alzheimer disease, and epsilon 3 is the neutral reference allele. Genotyping is therefore advised before treatment so that risk can be discussed and MRI monitoring planned.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man has had tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity for six years, responsive to levodopa. He now has progressive forgetfulness, inattention, and visual hallucinations. Which diagnosis best fits?
items.explanation: Dementia that arises well after established parkinsonism, conventionally more than one year after motor onset, is Parkinson disease dementia, with attentional and executive deficits and hallucinations. Dementia with Lewy bodies applies when cognitive symptoms precede or emerge within a year of motor symptoms. Progressive supranuclear palsy causes vertical gaze palsy and early falls. Hydrocephalus produces gait, urinary, and cognitive changes without levodopa-responsive parkinsonism.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has bilateral watershed infarcts. She sees only one object at a time in a scene, misreaches for objects she is looking at, and cannot voluntarily direct her gaze to targets. Where is the lesion?
items.explanation: Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and ocular motor apraxia form Balint syndrome, which results from bilateral damage to the parieto-occipital association cortex in the border zone between the middle and posterior cerebral arteries. Bilateral inferior temporal injury causes visual agnosia and prosopagnosia. Medial temporal injury produces amnesia. A unilateral angular gyrus lesion causes Gerstmann features. The preserved language and memory help distinguish it from diffuse dementia.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease still drives to the grocery store. His wife reports two recent near misses at intersections. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Allow unrestricted driving until a crash occurs
Arrange a formal on-road driving evaluation
Revoke the license permanently on diagnosis alone
Decide based on the MMSE score alone and his own assurance
items.explanation: A dementia diagnosis does not automatically end driving, but reported near misses raise concern about safety. A structured on-road assessment, with caregiver input, is the most valid way to judge fitness and plan a transition. Waiting for a crash puts others at risk. Permanent revocation based on diagnosis alone ignores variable function, and no single cognitive score reliably predicts crash risk. Local reporting laws also apply.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has progressive memory loss. His mother and maternal uncle developed the same illness in their late forties. Which gene is most commonly mutated in autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer disease?
items.explanation: Mutations in presenilin 1, a component of gamma-secretase, are the most frequent cause of autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer disease and are highly penetrant. Apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 is a risk modifier, not a deterministic cause, and does not produce a Mendelian pedigree. Tau mutations cause frontotemporal dementia, and prion protein mutations cause genetic prion disease with a faster, myoclonic course.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has sudden left leg weakness. When she flexes her right hip against resistance, the weak left hip extends firmly, although she cannot extend it on command. Which sign is this?
options: Lhermitte sign, supporting cervical cord demyelination
items.explanation: Involuntary hip extension of the weak leg when the other hip flexes against resistance is Hoover sign, a positive clinical sign of functional neurologic disorder, because automatic movement is preserved while voluntary effort fails. Babinski reflects an upper motor neuron lesion. Lhermitte describes electric sensations on neck flexion. Gowers sign describes climbing up the legs with the hands from the floor in proximal weakness.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man reports lifelong distractibility, missed deadlines, and losing items, beginning in grade school. He has no cardiac history. What is the best first-line pharmacologic treatment?
options: A long-acting stimulant such as methylphenidate
Lithium carbonate as a mood stabilizer for impulsivity
items.explanation: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder requires onset in childhood and is treated first with stimulants, which have the strongest effect, after screening for cardiac risk, blood pressure, and misuse. Atomoxetine is an alternative. Sertraline treats depression and anxiety without improving core inattention. Donepezil has no role, and lithium treats bipolar disorder. Behavioral coaching and organizational skills training can supplement medication.

items.stem: A clinic reviews four patients for anti-amyloid antibody therapy. Which patient is the most appropriate candidate?
options: A patient with moderate dementia and a negative amyloid PET scan
A patient on full anticoagulation with several cerebral microhemorrhages
A nursing home resident with severe dementia and confirmed amyloid
A 70-year-old with MCI and confirmed amyloid positivity
items.explanation: Anti-amyloid antibodies were studied in early symptomatic Alzheimer disease, meaning mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia with confirmed amyloid pathology, and benefit is modest. Negative amyloid imaging excludes the target. Anticoagulation and multiple microhemorrhages raise the risk of serious bleeding with amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Evidence in moderate to severe dementia is lacking, so treatment is not advised.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has several years of varied physical complaints, excessive worry about serious illness, and repeated normal test results. Which management is best?
options: Repeat advanced imaging every few months until she is reassured
Scheduled visits with one clinician and limited testing
Telling her firmly that the symptoms are imagined
items.explanation: Somatic symptom disorder is managed with a consistent, supportive relationship, planned short visits, limited low-yield testing, and cognitive behavioral therapy, which reduce distress and utilization. Repeated testing reinforces illness anxiety. Opioids add risk without benefit. Dismissing symptoms as imagined damages trust, because the suffering is real even when no structural disease is found. Treating coexisting anxiety or depression also helps.

items.stem: A pediatric neurologist evaluates a 6-year-old boy with delayed language, social difficulty, a long face with large ears, and an IQ of 62. His maternal uncle had similar difficulties. Which condition is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability?
items.explanation: Fragile X syndrome, from CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 on the X chromosome, is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and a leading single-gene cause of autism. Rett syndrome affects mainly girls and causes regression. Williams syndrome is a deletion with friendly behavior and cardiac disease. Down syndrome is usually sporadic from nondisjunction, not inherited.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man hospitalized after a stroke seems withdrawn and says he feels like a burden. What is the most appropriate approach to suicide risk?
options: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, and access to means
Avoid the topic because asking about suicide can introduce the idea to him
Rely on a signed no-suicide contract as the main safeguard
Defer the question until the depression has been treated
items.explanation: Direct, nonjudgmental inquiry does not increase suicidal ideation and is the foundation of risk assessment, including plan, intent, past attempts, and lethal means at home. Poststroke depression is common and raises risk. No-suicide contracts have no proven protective value. Waiting for treatment to work leaves a high-risk period unexamined. Positive screening should prompt safety planning, means restriction, and psychiatric referral.

items.stem: A 74-year-old retired teacher reports forgetting recent conversations. Her MoCA score is 23 of 30, with losses in delayed recall. She still manages her finances, medications, and driving without errors, as confirmed by her daughter. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease
Subjective cognitive decline without objective deficit
items.explanation: Objective memory loss on testing with preserved independence in daily activities defines mild cognitive impairment, and isolated recall loss makes it the amnestic type. Major neurocognitive disorder requires functional decline. Subjective decline is excluded because testing is abnormal. Benign forgetfulness of aging does not produce a below-threshold score with impaired delayed recall. Amnestic cases carry a higher yearly conversion rate to dementia.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has six months of excessive worry, muscle tension, and poor sleep that impair her work. She is concerned about dependence. Which treatment is best first line for long-term management?
options: An SSRI or SNRI combined with cognitive behavioral therapy
Quetiapine nightly with titration for anxiety and sleep disturbance
items.explanation: Generalized anxiety disorder is treated first with an SSRI or SNRI, with cognitive behavioral therapy, which are effective and carry no dependence risk. Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam work quickly but cause tolerance, withdrawal, and cognitive impairment, so they are reserved for short use. Quetiapine and zolpidem add sedation and metabolic or complex sleep behavior risks without treating the underlying disorder.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman develops persistent vomiting after bariatric surgery. She becomes confused, with nystagmus and gait ataxia, and receives thiamine only after several days. Weeks later she cannot form new memories and fills gaps with invented stories. Which structures are most injured in this chronic syndrome?
options: Mammillary bodies and anterior thalamic nuclei
Hippocampal CA1 neurons bilaterally and the dentate gyrus
items.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome follows untreated Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency, here due to malnutrition after surgery. It features dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation, from injury to the mammillary bodies, anterior thalamic nuclei, and Papez circuit. Hippocampal CA1 injury is seen after anoxia, entorhinal loss in early Alzheimer disease, and caudate atrophy in Huntington disease. Early parenteral thiamine is the key to preventing this outcome.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has episodes of whole-body shaking with eyes tightly closed, lasting ten minutes with waxing and waning intensity and preserved recall of events. Her routine EEG is normal. What is the best next test?
options: A serum prolactin level at six hours
A normal routine EEG as proof
MRI of the brain with contrast
Video-EEG monitoring that captures a typical event
items.explanation: Long events with eye closure, fluctuating motor activity, and recall suggest functional seizures, and the gold standard is video-EEG capturing an event without ictal EEG change. A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy. A prolactin level must be drawn within minutes to a few hours and has limited reliability. MRI evaluates structural disease and does not establish the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has sudden, uncontrollable bouts of laughing or crying that are out of proportion to his mood and embarrass him. Which treatment is approved for this condition?
items.explanation: Pseudobulbar affect, which follows corticobulbar disease in ALS, multiple sclerosis, and stroke, is treated with dextromethorphan-quinidine, with quinidine inhibiting CYP2D6 to raise dextromethorphan levels, and SSRIs or tricyclic agents are also effective. Haloperidol and lorazepam add sedation or extrapyramidal effects without addressing the mechanism. Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and has no evidence here. Recognizing the syndrome avoids misdiagnosing it as depression.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man draws a clock with numbers crowded on one side and hands that do not show the requested time. Which cognitive domains does this task primarily assess?
options: Primary visual acuity and color perception
items.explanation: Clock drawing requires planning, abstraction, number placement, and visuospatial construction, so errors reflect executive and visuospatial dysfunction, and they appear in many dementias including frontal, Lewy body, and vascular types. Episodic memory is assessed with delayed recall. Auditory comprehension and repetition are language functions. Visual acuity and color perception are sensory functions not tested by this drawing task.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with progressive amnestic cognitive impairment undergoes lumbar puncture to support an Alzheimer disease diagnosis. Which CSF profile is expected?
options: Elevated amyloid beta 42 with low phosphorylated tau
Normal amyloid and tau with oligoclonal bands
Low amyloid beta 42 with elevated phosphorylated tau
items.explanation: Alzheimer disease lowers CSF amyloid beta 42, because the peptide aggregates into plaques and is cleared from the fluid, while phosphorylated and total tau rise from neuronal injury and tangle formation. High amyloid with low tau is the reverse pattern. Oligoclonal bands point toward inflammatory disease such as multiple sclerosis. Low protein with high glucose is not a recognized degenerative profile.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has fluctuating confusion, tremor, and two seizures over weeks. Thyroid function is normal, anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are very high, and other causes are excluded. What is the best treatment?
items.explanation: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy with autoimmune thyroiditis, also called Hashimoto encephalopathy, presents with fluctuating cognition, seizures, and myoclonus despite normal thyroid function, and it responds to corticosteroids. The antibody titer does not reflect thyroid hormone status, so levothyroxine does not treat it. Antithyroid drugs and radioactive iodine address hyperthyroidism, which she does not have. Other encephalitides must be excluded first.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has new visual hallucinations, disorientation, and a fever. She has no psychiatric history. Which feature most strongly suggests a medical rather than primary psychiatric cause of her psychosis?
options: Commenting auditory voices heard with clear consciousness and orientation
Visual hallucinations with disorientation and abnormal vital signs
items.explanation: New psychosis after middle age, visual hallucinations, disorientation, and abnormal vital signs point to delirium or another medical, neurologic, or drug-related cause that needs urgent workup. Commenting voices with clear consciousness, long-standing decline, and flat affect with withdrawal are typical of primary schizophrenia, which seldom begins late in life and does not cause fever or disorientation.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has a severe depressive episode. Which treatment approach should generally be avoided as sole therapy?
items.explanation: Antidepressants used alone in bipolar I disorder can trigger mania or rapid cycling, so guidelines advise against monotherapy. Quetiapine, lurasidone, and the combination of olanzapine with fluoxetine have evidence in bipolar depression, as does lithium. Lamotrigine is useful for maintenance and for depressive poles, with slow titration to reduce rash risk. Mood should be monitored closely during any change.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man recovering from herpes simplex encephalitis puts inedible objects in his mouth, appears unusually docile, and makes inappropriate sexual comments. He does not recognize common objects by sight. Which lesion explains this syndrome?
options: Bilateral orbitofrontal cortex and ventral frontal lobes
items.explanation: Hyperorality, placidity, hypersexuality, and visual agnosia define Kluver-Bucy syndrome, caused by bilateral anterior temporal injury that includes the amygdalae, classically after herpes encephalitis. Orbitofrontal injury produces disinhibition without agnosia. Dorsolateral prefrontal injury causes executive failure and poor planning. Mammillary body injury produces an amnestic syndrome, not oral exploration or placidity. Management is supportive, with behavioral strategies and safety supervision.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has word-finding pauses and poor repetition of long sentences, but single-word comprehension and grammar are intact. MRI shows left temporoparietal atrophy. Which pathology most often underlies this presentation?
items.explanation: Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia reflects dysfunction of the left posterior temporal and inferior parietal regions, and most patients have Alzheimer disease pathology, which amyloid biomarkers can confirm. TDP-43 type C is typical of the semantic variant. Four-repeat tauopathies such as progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration commonly underlie the nonfluent variant. Lewy body pathology rarely produces an isolated aphasia.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with a family history of chorea has recently become slow to plan tasks and lost his place when multitasking. His memory for recent events is only mildly affected. Which cognitive domains are impaired earliest in this disorder?
items.explanation: Huntington disease produces a subcortical dementia from frontostriatal circuit dysfunction, with early slowing, poor planning, and impaired attention and set shifting. Naming, language comprehension, and reading are relatively spared until late stages. Remote memory is also preserved longer than new learning. Cognitive and psychiatric changes may precede the chorea by years, and the expanded CAG repeat confirms the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has progressive loss of word meaning. He asks, "What is a hammer?" when the word is spoken, reads "yacht" as "yatched," and speaks fluently without grammatical errors. MRI shows marked left anterior temporal atrophy. What is the diagnosis?
options: Nonfluent agrammatic variant primary progressive aphasia
Progressive apraxia of speech without aphasia
items.explanation: Fluent speech with loss of word and object meaning, surface dyslexia, and anterior temporal atrophy defines the semantic variant, most often with TDP-43 type C pathology. The nonfluent variant shows effortful, agrammatic speech with frontal insular atrophy. The logopenic variant shows word-finding pauses and poor sentence repetition. Isolated apraxia of speech produces articulation errors without loss of meaning.

items.stem: A 70-year-old right-handed woman has a large right middle cerebral artery stroke with left hemiplegia. She cheerfully states she can walk out of the hospital and that her left arm is fine. Which region is most often damaged in this condition?
items.explanation: Anosognosia for hemiplegia is unawareness of paralysis, and it most often follows large right hemisphere lesions involving the inferior parietal lobule and insula, often with hemineglect. It is more common and more severe with right-sided lesions than left. Left parietal lesions cause aphasia or Gerstmann features, occipital lesions cause visual field loss, and the left frontal operculum is part of the Broca region.

items.stem: Which long-term treatment has the best evidence for reducing suicide risk in a patient with bipolar disorder?
items.explanation: Lithium is the mood stabilizer with the strongest evidence for lowering suicide and self-harm in bipolar disorder, an effect that appears independent of mood stabilization. Carbamazepine and valproate lack comparable data, and gabapentin is not an established mood stabilizer. Because lithium is dangerous in overdose, prescribing should be limited and levels, renal function, and thyroid function monitored.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease misses two dialysis sessions. He is confused, with asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, and nausea. His urea level is markedly elevated. What is the best treatment?
items.explanation: Uremic encephalopathy produces confusion, asterixis, and myoclonus, and it resolves with dialysis, which removes the accumulated toxins. Benzodiazepines can worsen sedation and do not treat the cause. Thiamine alone does not address uremia. Valproate may suppress myoclonus but leaves the toxic state unchanged. Seizures can occur, and drugs cleared by the kidney need dose adjustment.
